newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION-From the Beehive-Nats' backs to the wall.
newsitem.headline: OPINION-From the Beehive-Nats' backs to the wall.

text.p: It was a "backs to the wall, chaps" mood in Cabinet on Monday, as the National government reeled from the onslaught of a revitalised, rejuvenated, up-market Helen Clark.

Meeting under the cloud of a thundering defeat for the prime minister in the leaders' debate, ministers could draw little solace from the latest One Network News Colmar Brunton poll which for the first time since the start of the election campaign showed that National and its allies had pulled ahead of their rivals on the Left.

That poll had been taken before the leaders' debate, and morale has slumped in the National camp, partly because of Jim Bolger's lacklustre performance, and also because of the petulant reaction to the way the audience was stacked.

Meanwhile, in the Labour camp, there is jubilation at how Opposition Leader Helen Clark has, in effect, captured the campaign, making her goal of becoming prime minister after October looking daily more achievable.

Labour has moved up into second place in at least two major polls, and looks to be within reach of its target of at least 25 percent in the party vote, which would entitle it to 30 seats in the new Parliament, sufficient with support from the Alliance and New Zealand First to form the first MMP government.
Meanwhile the NZ Institute of Economic Research predicts that the exchange rate could fall after a Centre-Left election victory, but could come back as interest rates rise.

While the institute tips a centre-left coalition, Electoral Reform Coalition chairman Tony Day of Christchurch says commentators should not write off a National/NZ First coalition. He says National historically had shown itself to be pragmatic in the pursuit of power and able to change policy.
But Day ignores the ferocious hatred that exists between National's leader and his onetime colleague, now bitter enemy Winston Peters.
Labour is gearing up for interparty talks, with Helen Clark indicating that she will use, among others, former Prime Minister Mike Moore to help negotiate the coalition arrangement.
Moore, who has rejoined the Labour front-bench after months of isolation, expects to be Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade in a Clark-led coalition.

His usefulness to Clark is that he has very close links to several MPs in New Zealand First, including onetime Labour MP Jack Elder, and onetime National MP Peter McCardle, both of whom made no secret that they would have joined a Moore-led party, along probably with disgraced Hawkes Bay MP Michael Laws, who is now NZ First's chief strategic adviser.

Moore says there are basic policies, priorities and principles that Labour, the Alliance and NZ First share: a commitment to better, cheaper, public health: a commitment to do better for tertiary students; opposition to market rents for state housing.

According to Moore, parties of the Left should now be quietly considering policies, programmes, personalities and portfolios that will have to be negotiated. The interesting point that is emerging is how Moore has moved back into the limelight, and appears to be displacing Labour's deputy leader Michael Cullen in Clark's inner circles.

In a Labour-led coalition, with Clark as prime minister, and Moore as Foreign Minister, a coalition partner such as NZ First could demand the posts of deputy prime minister and finance minister. That could effectively squeeze Cullen out of the top echelon.
It would be even more complex if the Alliance, despite its pre-election stance on not joining any coalition, did in fact reach a deal with Labour, as Helen Clark urged in the leaders' debate.

That would mean the Alliance could insist on two or three top Cabinet portfolios, which for example include Labour, Health and Conservation. Such permutations might receive more attention as the election race goes down to the wire.
(Note - The views expressed in the above article are those of the author and are not attributable to Reuters.)
